seo.title: Karmic tail 6 20 5 compatibility: Lovers, Judgement and Hierophant
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 20 5 compatibility: a choice made by two, the verdict of two families and whose law the couple lives by, read through Manzoni's The Betrothed.

title: The 6-20-5 karmic tail in compatibility: who marries the couple?
short: The 6-20-5 karmic tail in compatibility is made of The Lovers, Judgement and The Hierophant, and it hides a question couples rarely ask out loud: when does a union become real — when two people have said "yes" to each other, or when other people have accepted that "yes"? The cards answer in order. The couple enters its task through a choice of its own, passes through the judgement of two families and of its own conscience, and learns the main thing: to live by a law written by both of them — not by someone else's law, and not by the law of one of the two.

sections.h2: This wedding shall not happen: a novel about a couple nobody will marry
paragraphs: On the evening of 7 November 1628 a village priest, Don Abbondio, is walking home along a road above Lake Como, and at a fork two armed men of the local lord, Don Rodrigo, are waiting for him. They give him one sentence: "This wedding shall not happen — not tomorrow, not ever." The wedding is set for tomorrow. The groom is Renzo Tramaglino, a silk spinner; the bride is Lucia Mondella. Everything between them is settled, the families agree, the guests are invited.

Then come thirty-eight chapters. Renzo and Lucia try to marry on their own, flee their village and lose each other. Lucia is hidden in a convent and then abducted; Renzo is caught up in a bread riot in Milan and flees across the border of the duchy; then comes the plague of 1630. And in the last chapter the couple is married by the very same Don Abbondio. The novel came out in 1827, the final version in 1840, and Italian schools still teach it: modern literary Italian owes a great deal to this book.

The 6-20-5 tail reads in it as three acts. **Act one — The Lovers:** two people choose each other and try to become husband and wife by their own words. **Act two — Judgement:** separation, family, fear, a night in which the biggest decisions are made and unmade, and a plague after which each of them looks at themselves again. **Act three — The Hierophant:** who will join these two, and under what law — and what rule the couple will draw up for itself at the end.

sections.h2: The entry: "the priest has to be there, but he needn't be willing"
paragraphs: The plan comes not from the bride or the groom but from Lucia's mother, Agnese. She explains the old way: two reliable witnesses, and everything done in front of the priest. "The man says: Signor Curate, this is my wife; the woman says: Signor Curate, this is my husband" — and the marriage is done, "as holy as if the Pope himself had made it". And the key line: "You do need the priest, yes, but he needn't want to; it's enough that he's there."
Lucia is against it. "If a thing isn't right, it shouldn't be done," she says, and also: "I want to be your wife, but by the straight road, in the fear of God, at the altar."

This is the entry to the 6-20-5 couple's task, packed into one conversation. Both want the same thing — to marry. Where they part is the question of what makes a union a union. For Renzo two sentences, said about each other, are enough. Lucia needs the altar. And neither of them is wrong: The Lovers are a choice two people make, The Hierophant is the form that choice is looking for. For Lisovskaya, point M is what the couple strives for, its shared wishes and agreements. But it sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. In a 6-20-5 couple the resistance runs both ways: "we decided, and nobody tells us what to do" — and "until we are recognised, it isn't real".

That night they go to Don Abbondio anyway. Renzo manages to say: "Signor Curate, before these witnesses: this is my wife." Lucia gets out only "and this…" — the priest throws the cloth from his table over her head, the sexton rings the alarm bell, the whole village wakes up. The bride's words break off in the middle, and those were the very words that were meant to make them husband and wife.

Today that evening looks different. A couple quietly signs the register and presents the parents with a done deal, announces the wedding date as settled, moves in together without asking anyone. Sometimes this is freedom. Sometimes it is the same surprise wedding: a decision meant to shield the union from other people's judgement becomes the first thing other people judge.

In the couple's reading the same point M also appears in the sphere "Relationship and common language", under the caption "Common language". In every 6-20-5 couple The Lovers stand there too. In the novel the common language literally passes through go-betweens. Renzo and Agnese cannot read or write: a scribe writes Renzo's letters for him, and Agnese has them read to her by a cousin. Manzoni describes it with bitter precision: the scribe "partly understands, partly misunderstands", and afterwards the two sides argue about what the words mean. The downside of the Six at the entry often looks exactly like this: two people talking to each other through third parties — through mothers, friends, retellings, screenshots. Other downsides walk beside it: the picture of "we'll never be like them" that does not survive the first quarrel, and an insecurity that looks for reassurance now in jealousy, now in other people's approval.

sections.h2: A clue: who makes a marriage — the two, or the witness?
paragraphs: Agnese did not make anything up. In 1563 the Council of Trent, in the decree Tametsi, declared valid only a marriage contracted before the parish priest and two or three witnesses. But the law required the priest's presence, not his consent. People used this: they turned up at the priest's door without warning, spoke the words in front of him, and the marriage counted as made. In Italy this was called matrimonio a sorpresa, a marriage by surprise. The loophole was closed only by the decree Ne temere, issued in 1907 and in force from Easter 1908: from then on the priest himself had to ask for the couple's consent and receive it. Agnese's trick lived in church law for almost three and a half centuries.

Beneath this legal history lies a deeper question. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (§ 1623) says that in the Latin Church the spouses themselves perform the sacrament: "the spouses, as ministers of Christ's grace, mutually confer upon each other the sacrament of Matrimony by expressing their consent before the Church." The priest is a witness. In the Eastern rite it is different: the priest, having received the consent, crowns the bride and groom. The Russian word for a church wedding, venchanie, comes from venets, "crown", and keeps exactly this answer. Two churches answer differently the question of who makes a marriage a marriage.

A 6-20-5 couple carries both answers at once. The Lovers say: a union is made by the two. The Hierophant says: a union needs a form and a witness. And Judgement in the middle shows what happens between these two truths: the road from one to the other runs through the family, through fear and through a second look.

sections.h2: Don Abbondio's Latin: a rule spoken so as not to be understood
paragraphs: In the morning Renzo comes to be married, and Don Abbondio, sick with fear, spins excuses, then suddenly switches to Latin: "Error, conditio, votum, cognatio, crimen, Cultus disparitas, vis, ordo, ligamen, honestas, Si sis affinis…" It is a schoolroom rhyme of the canon lawyers, a list of impediments to marriage: error, unfree status, vow, kinship, crime, difference of faith, force, holy orders, an existing marriage, public propriety, affinity. Renzo cuts him short: "Are you making fun of me? What do I want with your Latin?" In Italian he does not say "Latin" but the mocking latinorum, and the word entered the language. The Treccani dictionary defines it as the Latin of someone who does not want to be understood — and, more broadly, as any speech made obscure on purpose.

There is a detail that is easy to miss. Don Abbondio stops at "Si sis affinis". After the Council of Trent the rhyme went on with the words "si clandestinus" — if the marriage is secret — and the next line began "Raptave sit mulier" — or if the woman has been abducted. The priest falls silent one word away from the plot. A few chapters later the couple will attempt a secret marriage, then Lucia will be abducted, and the "votum", the vow he did pronounce, will come back into the story from Lucia's own lips. A list read out to scare them off becomes this couple's road.

This is what the Hierophant of the main task looks like at its worst. Don Abbondio is no villain. Manzoni calls him an earthenware pot forced to travel in the company of iron ones, and later he himself admits to the cardinal: "Courage — a man can't give it to himself." Behind the Latin stands fear. In a couple, Latin sounds like this: "that's how it's done", "normal people do it this way", "in our family we don't do that", "Mum knows best". The rule is spoken not to explain but to end the conversation. One partner lectures: "you're doing it all wrong". The other quietly does it their own way. Someone runs the shared money "out of care", someone tries to remake the partner to their own family's standard. Lisovskaya lists all these stories on the downside of the Five; in life they seldom look like a quarrel over principles — more often like an argument about where to spend the holidays and who decides what to save for.

Benebell Wen describes the upright Hierophant as someone who "relies on another, a figure of authority or an institution, to define ... what is right and wrong"; the reversed Hierophant "defines right and wrong by self-determination". And she adds a line any couple with this tail can use: "We are not the keeper of others." Waite agrees with the formula that the Hierophant is "the power of the keys". Keys are sometimes needed to lock things. Don Abbondio uses them only that way. The novel will show their other use.

sections.h2: The middle: Judgement — the night when verdicts are passed
paragraphs: The middle of the novel coincides with the middle of the tail. After the failed night the couple separates. Lucia and her mother take refuge in a convent in Monza. Renzo goes to Milan, falls into a bread riot, makes a speech in the square, lingers too long at an inn, is arrested, is freed by the crowd and flees across the river Adda to a cousin, where he lives under another name. And Lucia, on Don Rodrigo's orders, is abducted and taken to the castle of a robber lord whom the novel simply calls the Unnamed.

That night two verdicts are passed in the castle. Lucia, alone in a locked room, vows to the Madonna to remain a virgin: "I renounce for ever that poor man of mine." She does not say Renzo's name. And the lord of the castle cannot sleep. Towards morning he hears distant festive bells, sees people in their best clothes hurrying down the valley, and asks himself: "What is all this joy? What have they all got to be glad about?" That same morning he will meet the cardinal and come out a different man. Waite writes of Judgement as a summons "heard and answered from within"; in the novel it sounds as ordinary church bells.

For Lisovskaya, the Twentieth energy is family and lineage. In the novel the family stands in every scene of the couple. Agnese invents the surprise wedding, goes everywhere with her daughter, has her letters read by a cousin. A cousin saves Renzo from destitution. The role of father to both is played by a Capuchin friar, Fra Cristoforo, whom everyone calls "Padre". For a 6-20-5 couple the middle of the road also runs through the families. The first holidays at the parents' and the question of whose traditions come first. A partner who decides nothing without Mum. A union the families approved — or didn't. A difference in age, standing or faith that the families notice before the lovers do. And at its best — what Lisovskaya puts on the strong side of the Twenty: the ability to forgive mistakes, support even when the partner is wrong, and a family that takes in a stranger as one of its own.

Then the plague comes. Renzo catches it and survives. In Milan a crowd takes him for an untore, an "anointer" — someone supposedly smearing the walls with contagion — and he escapes by jumping onto the cart of the gravediggers carrying away the dead. The false verdict of a crowd preoccupied Manzoni so much that he attached to the final edition of the novel the History of the Column of Infamy — about the real Milan trial of summer 1630, when the barber Gian Giacomo Mora and the sanitary commissioner Guglielmo Piazza were executed as anointers on a baseless accusation, and a column of shame was put up on the site of Mora's demolished house. Judgement has two faces: the summons that wakes, and the verdict passed too soon.

In the plague hospital Fra Cristoforo leads Renzo to the dying Don Rodrigo: "It may be punishment, it may be mercy." And Renzo, who more than once dreamed of getting even with Don Rodrigo, says: "I forgive him! I truly forgive him, I forgive him for ever!" In the middle of the book two "for evers" are spoken: Lucia renounces for ever, Renzo forgives for ever. One closes the road, the other opens it.

Here lies a clue in the numbers as well. In a personal destiny matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of its ends, and a person with ends 6 and 5 would get 11, Strength, in the middle. Couples can have that tail too — 6-11-5. But a couple's middle is built not from the ends but from the middles of the two partners, most often 3 + 17, and the result is 20 — a middle that a personal matrix with these ends never has. One person would travel from love to law through Strength, through endurance and will. Two travel through Judgement: through verdicts that are passed and then reviewed.

sections.h2: The main task: one person's vow for two
paragraphs: The plague hospital, chapter thirty-six. Renzo finds Lucia: she has survived the plague. And he hears from her: there is a vow; forget me. Renzo is in despair, and then proposes the thing that changes everything: "Promise Her that the first daughter we have, we'll name Maria." Fra Cristoforo hears them both out and tells Lucia the essential thing: she could not offer to God "the will of another, to whom she was already bound by her word". And "with the authority I have from the Church" he declares her free of the vow.

The whole main task of 6-20-5 is in this scene. A rule for two cannot be set by one. Lucia's vow is sincere, made in terror, at night, alone — and it disposes of Renzo's life without Renzo. In couples such vows sound ordinary: "we will never live near your mother", "there will be no children until I decide", "I'm never going to your family's again". One person makes them, in a moment of fear or hurt, and they bind both. The task of the Five in a couple, as Lisovskaya puts it, is to reach a shared decision about the family and to hold opposites in balance without lecturing. Renzo shows what this looks like: he does not argue with the vow, he turns it into a promise of two — "we have", "we'll name".

And here are the keys. The Gospel formula of the power of the keys: "whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven" (Matthew 16:19). To release someone from a vow is to loose a knot. Fra Cristoforo says the same in Italian: "sciolta" — untied. Don Abbondio used the keys to lock; Fra Cristoforo used them to untie. A couple's Hierophant can be either of the two.

And one more clue from the same canon-law vocabulary. Don Abbondio's list goes back to a rhyme by the canonist Tancred, written early in the thirteenth century, and that rhyme opens with the line "Ecclesiae vetitum, tempus, sponsalia, votum": betrothal and vow stand side by side in it. The title of the novel is the same word: I promessi sposi, "the betrothed". In the plague hospital the betrothal and the vow collide, and the betrothal wins — because two people made it.

The numbers say the same thing. The 6-20-5 tail is made from six combinations of the partners' personal tails, and not one of them contains The Hierophant or Judgement. Both cards are born only in the sum. This couple's main task belongs to neither partner alone — exactly what Fra Cristoforo explained to Lucia.

And the wedding happens "by the mouth of Don Abbondio". The form has not changed: the same priest, the same rite, the same church. What has changed is the couple's attitude to the form. Now it is a witness, not a wall.

sections.h2: "The juice of the whole story": the rule a couple draws up for itself
paragraphs: The last chapter. Renzo loves to tell what he has learned: "I've learned not to get mixed up in riots; I've learned not to make speeches in the square; I've learned not to lift my elbow too often; I've learned not to hold a door knocker when there are hotheads about." Every item is one of his own mistakes from the novel, named out loud. Lucia replies: "I didn't go looking for trouble — trouble came looking for me."

And then, Manzoni writes, "after long debating and searching together" they concluded: troubles often come because we have given them cause; but the most cautious and innocent conduct is not enough to keep them away; and when they come — "by our fault or without fault" — trust in God softens them and makes them useful for a better life. Manzoni calls this conclusion "the juice of the whole story".

Here is The Hierophant at its best. It is a teaching, but one written by two people, from their own experience, without hunting for the guilty one: "by our fault or without fault". Wen writes of Judgement: "An important life lesson will be learned." Of The Hierophant — that it is about "the pedagogy of wisdom". Renzo has both. His "I've learned" is the lesson of Judgement. And his decision that all his children will learn to read and write — "since this roguery exists, they might as well get the good of it too" — is the Hierophant's pedagogy: the Latin that locked the door in chapter two becomes a family tradition of literacy. Their first child is a girl, and she is named Maria. The vow is untied, the promise of two is kept. (This last link is our reading, not Manzoni's words.)

The strong version of the 6-20-5 tail looks like this: the couple has rules of its own, said in plain words; after every storm the two review them together; the families stand nearby as witnesses, not as judges.

sections.h2: How the 6-20-5 tail is formed: the calculation and the clues in the numbers
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The example uses the dates 05.12.1975 and 05.11.1975.

The first partner has day 5, month 12, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Main task D = 5 + 12 + 22 = 39 → 12, centre = 5 + 12 + 22 + 12 = 51 → 6, entry M = 12 + 6 = 18, middle N = 18 + 12 = 30 → 3. Personal tail: 18-3-12. The second has day 5, month 11, year 22: D = 38 → 11, centre 49 → 13, M = 11 + 13 = 24 → 6, N = 6 + 11 = 17. Personal tail: 6-17-11.
Running through every date produced several facts, and each one is a clue.

ul: **The tail is rare, but not exceptional.** It occurs in roughly one couple in 232 (0.432%) and ranks 62nd of the 97 couple tails.

**It is usually built from the same tails.** In 85% of such couples one partner has the personal tail 18-3-12 and the other 6-17-11, as in the example. Another 5% are two 21-10-16 tails, 4% are 3-13-10 and 3-7-22; the remaining three combinations are rarer. None of the six contains 20 or 5: this couple's Judgement and Hierophant appear only in the sum.
**No single person has this tail.** In a personal matrix the entry M = main task D + centre. For the entry to be 6 when D = 5, the centre would have to be 1 or 19, and no person has such a centre.

**The Sun is almost always at the centre.** In 79.3% of such couples the centre of the chart is 19, The Sun; in 20.7% it is 10, The Wheel of Fortune. No date gives a personal matrix centre 19: this atmosphere exists only between two people.

**The couple's values.** In the spiritual purpose there is 3, The Empress, in 54.9%; 21, The World, in 24.7%; 12, The Hanged Man, in 20.4%. In the example it is The Empress. Our reading: the law this couple is heading towards matters not for its own sake but for the home it holds up — as in Manzoni, whose book ends not with a ceremony but with children.

paragraphs: The example also has coincidences of its own that other couples may not share: The Hierophant also stands at the point "What to create together", and The Lovers at the point "What fills". Couple tails made of the same three numbers in a different order do not exist.

sections.h2: What a couple with this tail can do
paragraphs: This is not a prediction and not a verdict: the tail does not say whether there will be a wedding, a church ceremony or a divorce. It shows the question through which the couple grows. The novel suggests a few moves.

ul: **Tell the couple's own rules from Latin.** It helps to say out loud, at least once, whose each rule in the house is: mine, yours, Mum's, ours. A rule that cannot be explained in plain words, only pronounced to end an argument, is Don Abbondio's Latin.

**Make no vows for two.** Every "never" and "not for anything" that affects both is decided by both. If one partner has already promised something in fear or hurt, the way out is Renzo's: turn one person's vow into an agreement of two.
**Family as witnesses, not judges.** Agnese's formula works here too: for the family "it's enough to be there". It can be invited, heard and respected, but the decision stays inside the couple.

**Review the verdicts.** This couple's quarrels often end in a verdict: "you always", "your family never". Judgement in the middle of the tail is a reminder that a verdict can be reviewed and that forgiveness is a decision too.

**After every storm, a "juice of the story" of its own.** One sentence drawn up together: what was learned, without hunting for the guilty one. Over time such sentences add up to the couple's own law — the very thing The Hierophant in the main task asks it to create.

paragraphs: Form is not the enemy. Lucia wanted the altar and was no less right than Renzo. A 6-20-5 couple does not choose between love and form: its task is to make the form its own.

ul: Alessandro Manzoni, The Betrothed (I promessi sposi), 1840 edition, chapters I, II, VI, VIII, XXI, XXV, XXVII, XXXIII, XXXV, XXXVI, XXXVIII; quotations in our own translation from the Italian. History of the Column of Infamy (Storia della colonna infame), appended to the 1840 edition.
Council of Trent, Session XXIV (1563), decree Tametsi; decree Ne temere (1907, in force from 1908).
Catholic Encyclopedia, "Canonical Impediments": Tancred's rhyme and its post-Tridentine version.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911); Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015); Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024).

**6 · The Lovers — "Entry to the task".** The couple is set in motion by a choice two people made: "we decided". This is their common language — and their first resistance: "nobody tells us what to do".

**20 · Judgement — "Middle of the task".** The road runs through the family line: parents, their blessing and their disapproval, old family scores. And through a review after which each partner owns their share of the mistakes.

**5 · The Hierophant — "Main task".** Whose rulebook the union lives by. At its worst: the elders' rules, lectures, one partner deciding for both. At its best: rules and traditions of the couple's own, drawn together from their own experience.

intro: This tail has a book in which it is lived out from beginning to end: Alessandro Manzoni's The Betrothed. The wedding is set on the first page and held on the last, and everything in between is laid out in the order of the three cards.

faq.q: What does the 6-20-5 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail with The Lovers as the entry to the task, Judgement in the middle and The Hierophant as the main task. The couple is joined by its own choice, passes through the judgement of the families and a review of its own decisions, and learns to live by a shared law written by both — not by the elders' rules and not by the will of one partner.

faq.q: Is the 6-20-5 tail bad for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail speaks about tasks, not about the fate of the union. For Lisovskaya the main task is read mostly through its downside: what the couple cannot yet manage. Here that means other people's rules, lectures and one partner deciding for both. The same card at its best gives the couple traditions of its own and the ability to agree without Latin.

faq.q: Does such a couple have to marry in church or register the marriage?
faq.a: No. The Hierophant does not prescribe a rite. It asks whose law the couple lives by. One couple needs an altar, another a signature at the registry office, a third an agreement with no witnesses at all. The task is for both to make this choice, not one partner or somebody's family.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail Judgement and not Strength?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle is the sum of the ends: 6 + 5 = 11, Strength. In a couple's matrix the middle is built from the middles of the two partners, most often 3 + 17 = 20. That is why this couple's road runs not through one person's endurance but through a review of two people's decisions.

faq.q: Can one person have the 6-20-5 tail?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry M = main task D + centre. For the entry to be 6 when D = 5, the centre would have to be 1 or 19, and no person has such a centre. The 6-20-5 tail exists only for a couple.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. Running through every date gives not a single couple with any rearrangement of 6, 20 and 5. So the 6-20-5 tail has no twin with the same cards in different roles.

report: Renzo and Lucia's wedding was set on the first page of the novel and held on the last, and they were married by the very priest who had refused to marry them. Between those pages lie the thirty-eight chapters of Alessandro Manzoni's The Betrothed, and the 6-20-5 tail lies in them whole, in the order of its cards. The Lovers at the entry: two people chose each other themselves. Judgement in the middle: separation, family, a night of verdicts. The Hierophant in the main task: under whose law these two will become husband and wife — and under whose law they will live.

report.h3: The juice of the whole story

report: In the last chapter Renzo lists what he has learned: not to get mixed up in riots, not to make speeches in the square, not to lift his elbow too often. Lucia replies: "I didn't go looking for trouble — trouble came looking for me." And "after long debating and searching together" they draw up a shared rule: troubles often come because we have given them cause, but the most cautious and innocent conduct is not enough to keep them away; and when they come — "by our fault or without fault" — trust in God softens them and makes them useful for a better life. Manzoni calls this conclusion "the juice of the whole story".

This is **The Hierophant at its best**: a teaching written by two people, from their own experience and without hunting for the guilty one. Renzo decides that all his children will learn to read and write — the Latin that locked the door becomes a family tradition of literacy. Their first daughter is named Maria. The strong version of a couple with this tail is one whose rules are said in plain words and reviewed together after every storm, with the family standing nearby as a witness, not a judge.

unit.title: A witness, not a wall

captions.M: To choose each other yourselves: “we decided”
captions.N: To pass the families' judgement and review your verdicts
captions.D: To live by rules written by both of you, not by one

unit.meaning: Your task is to set the rules for two together: no “that's how it's done” Latin and no vows one of you makes for both.
